call.result:
arXiv ID: 2609.01590
Title: TeV Higgsino Dark Matter from LZ Nuclear Recoil to Fermi-LAT Gamma Rays
Authors: Lei Wu, Yang Zhang, Bin Zhu
Year: 2026
Abstract: The excess of high-energy nuclear recoils, which was recently reported by the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, together with the Fermi-LAT Galactic-Center preference, suggests new physics beyond the standard model (SM). One of the minimal extensions of the SM is to introduce a fermionic electroweak doublet in which the lightest neutral component can play the role of a stable dark matter particle. We show that the minimal higgsino dark matter can offer a common origin for both excesses. The inferred mass splitting, however, depends on the local dark matter velocity distribution, and including the high-velocity tail generated by the gravitational influence of the Large Magellanic Cloud yields $δ_m =481$--$519~\mathrm{keV}$ for $m_χ=1000$--$1183~\mathrm{GeV}$ at $1σ$ level. Near elastic-scattering blind spots, solar-captured higgsinos fail to reach thermal equilibrium, weakening their annihilation signal, so that ten years of IceCube data exclude $δ_m \lesssim 475~\mathrm{keV}$ at 90% C.L. The viable parameter space can be tested through the associated gamma-ray line, which is within the projected reach of CTAO.

call.result:
arXiv ID: 2609.07807
Title: Not so good $ν$s for Higgsino dark matter as LZ excess: stringent limits from Super-Kamiokande and IceCube
Authors: Debajit Bose, Akash Kumar Saha, Deep Jyoti Das, Rinchen Sherpa, Abhijeet Singh, Durba Ghosh, Jaya Doliya, Subhadip Bouri, Biprajit Mondal, Ranjini Mondol, Nirmal Raj, Ranjan Laha
Year: 2026
Abstract: The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) collaboration has recently reported a single nuclear recoil event at a high recoil energy of about 250 keV. This has been interpreted as inelastic scattering of dark matter that is a supersymmetric Higgsino with a mass splitting between the neutral states of a few 100 keV. Such dark matter may be captured at high recoil in the Sun through scattering on heavy elements in it, and annihilate to $W^+W^-$ and $ZZ$, in turn giving rise to a neutrino flux detectable on Earth. Using measurements of atmospheric electron- and muon-neutrino fluxes by Super-Kamiokande and IceCube, we constrain thermal and non-thermal Higgsino dark matter, excluding inter-state mass splittings $\lesssim 557$ keV. This disfavors Higgsino-like interpretations of the LZ event for standard halo velocities.

call.result:
arXiv ID: 2609.09830
Title: Radiative Corrections to the Direct Detection of Inelastic Scattering of Higgsino-like Neutralino Dark Matter
Authors: Arindam Chatterjee, Debottam Das, Syed Adil Pasha, Alexander Pukhov, Rahul Puri
Year: 2026
Abstract: The direct detection (DD) of Higgsino-like dark matter (DM) through inelastic scattering processes may provide a promising avenue, along with the elastic scattering, when the mass splitting between the neutral Higgsino pairs is extremely tiny. The mass splitting can be reduced further by adopting the on-shell renormalization for the neutral and charged Higgsinos in the MSSM. Moreover, all the one-loop electroweak (EW) corrections to the three-point vertices for the neutralino(s)-Higgs interactions have been considered, while both elastic and inelastic DM-nucleon scattering cross-sections have been calculated primarily through Higgs exchange. Subsequently, the expected number of scattering events in the latest LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) DD experiment are also computed. Our results highlight a few scenarios in which the inelastic component may exceed the corresponding elastic component, leading to enhanced direct detection scattering rates.

Abstract: We report results of a search for nuclear recoils induced by weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) dark matter using the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) two-phase xenon time projection chamber. This analysis uses a total exposure of $4.2\pm0.1$ tonne-years from 280 live days of LZ operation, of which $3.3\pm0.1$ tonne-years and 220 live days are new. A technique to actively tag background electronic recoils from $^{214}$Pb $β$ decays is featured for the first time. Enhanced electron-ion recombination is observed in two-neutrino double electron capture decays of $^{124}$Xe, representing a noteworthy new background. After removal of artificial signal-like events injected into the data set to mitigate analyzer bias, we find no evidence for an excess over expected backgrounds. World-leading constraints are placed on spin-independent (SI) and spin-dependent WIMP-nucleon cross sections for masses $\geq$9 GeV/$c^2$. The strongest SI exclusion set is $2.2\times10^{-48}$ cm$^{2}$ at the 90% confidence level and the best SI median sensitivity achieved is $5.1\times10^{-48}$ cm$^{2}$, both for a mass of 40 GeV/$c^2$.

Abstract: The design and performance of the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) detector is described as of March 2015 in this Conceptual Design Report. LZ is a second-generation dark-matter detector with the potential for unprecedented sensitivity to weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) of masses from a few GeV/c2 to hundreds of TeV/c2. With total liquid xenon mass of about 10 tonnes, LZ will be the most sensitive experiment for WIMPs in this mass region by the end of the decade. This report describes in detail the design of the LZ technical systems. Expected backgrounds are quantified and the performance of the experiment is presented. The LZ detector will be located at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota. The organization of the LZ Project and a summary of the expected cost and current schedule are given.

Abstract: We report results from searches for new physics models through electron recoils using data collected by the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment during its first two science runs, with a total exposure of 4.2 tonne-years. The observed data are consistent with a background-only hypothesis. Constraints are derived for electromagnetic interactions of solar neutrinos, solar axion-like particles (ALPs), mirror dark matter, and the absorption of bosonic dark matter candidates. The inverse Primakoff process for 57Fe de-excitation solar ALPs is considered for the first time. These results represent the most stringent constraints to date on keV-scale Primakoff and 57Fe solar ALPs, bosonic dark matter, mirror dark matter, and neutrino millicharge, while remaining competitive for the other signal models investigated.

Abstract: We describe the Dark Energy Survey (DES), a proposed optical-near infrared survey of 5000 sq. deg of the South Galactic Cap to ~24th magnitude in SDSS griz, that would use a new 3 sq. deg CCD camera to be mounted on the Blanco 4-m telescope at Cerro Telolo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO). The survey data will allow us to measure the dark energy and dark matter densities and the dark energy equation of state through four independent methods: galaxy clusters, weak gravitational lensing tomography, galaxy angular clustering, and supernova distances. These methods are doubly complementary: they constrain different combinations of cosmological model parameters and are subject to different systematic errors. By deriving the four sets of measurements from the same data set with a common analysis framework, we will obtain important cross checks of the systematic errors and thereby make a substantial and robust advance in the precision of dark energy measurements.

Abstract: Dark matter interacts gravitationally, but it presumably interacts weakly through other channels, especially with respect to regular luminous matter. We look at different ways in which dark matter may couple to other fields. We briefly review some example approaches in the literature for modeling the coupling between dark energy and dark matter and examine the possibility of an arguably better-motivated approach via non-minimal coupling between a scalar field and the Ricci scalar, which is necessary for renormalization of the scalar field in curved space-time. We also show an example of a theory beyond the Standard Model in which dark matter is uniquely connected to the inflaton, and we use observational astrophysical constraints to specify an upper bound on the dark matter mass. In turn, this mass constraint implies a limit on the unification scale of the theory, a decoupling scale of the theory, and the number of $e$-folds of inflation allowed.

brief.summary: The pure higgsino, a Dirac-like electroweak doublet whose neutral states are split by a small Majorana mass, is a standard WIMP target. Its mass is fixed by requiring the thermal freeze-out abundance to match the Planck value Omega h^2 of about 0.12. That puts it near 1.0-1.2 TeV; the commonly quoted 1.1 TeV is background knowledge, and none of the returned abstracts state it. Sommerfeld enhancement and coannihilation with the charged state are needed to compute this mass precisely (1411.6930, 1008.2905). Bound-state effects are claimed to be important mainly above a few TeV (1407.7874). For elastic spin-independent scattering, the pure higgsino lies below the LZ 4.2 tonne-year limits (2410.17036; best SI limit 2.2e-48 cm^2, set at 40 GeV) and the XENONnT limits (2303.14729), because tree-level Z exchange is turned off by the inelastic mass splitting delta_m. The cross-section limits near 1.1 TeV are not given in these abstracts and must be read from the published curves. A burst of 2026 papers concerns a single LZ nuclear-recoil candidate at E_R = 248 keV (3.4 sigma local, 2.6 sigma global, from a 2.84 tonne-year exposure). It has been read as higgsino inelastic scattering with delta_m around 480-520 keV for m_chi = 1000-1183 GeV, which is exactly the thermal relic window (2609.01590). Neutrino constraints from dark matter captured and annihilating in the Sun are in tension with this reading: Super-K plus IceCube exclude delta_m below about 557 keV, which disfavors it for standard halo velocities (2609.07807), while IceCube alone excludes below about 475 keV once velocity effects near the blind spot are included (2609.01590). Other papers try to rescue the window (2610.03692) or look at boosted, non-halo explanations (2609.06890). Summary of where the higgsino stands: the thermal 1.0-1.2 TeV higgsino is not excluded by elastic xenon limits. It is directly testable through inelastic Z-mediated scattering only for delta_m up to a few hundred keV, where LZ's high-recoil sensitivity, solar-neutrino limits and the CTAO gamma-ray line together close in on the remaining parameter space.

Warning: I had only search and metadata tools. No inelastic-DM or relic-density calculator was available to me, so no relic densities or rates were computed here. The planner needs to send those calculations to the compute tools.
No Planck 2018 parameters paper was returned by my searches. The Omega h^2 = 0.120 +/- 0.001 value is standard but needs a citation retrieved before it is quoted.
Exact LZ/XENONnT limits at 1-1.2 TeV are not in the abstracts. The published limit curves (from data releases or full texts) are needed to make a quantitative comparison.

Most papers on the LZ 248 keV event are from 2026 (2609.xxxxx and 2610.xxxxx IDs) and recent. Several are v1 preprints whose results conflict (475 vs 557 keV exclusion), so treat their conclusions as provisional.
Generic searches return a lot of irrelevant material (DES, LSST, directional detection). Specific terms such as 'higgsino', 'inelastic', '248 keV' and 'LZ' work much better.

literature.title: Heavy neutralino relic abundance with Sommerfeld enhancements - a study of pMSSM scenarios

literature.title: Thermal abundance of non-relativistic relics with Sommerfeld enhancement

literature.title: Bound-state formation for thermal relic dark matter and unitarity
literature.relevance: Bound-state effects on relic abundance. The abstract says they matter mainly above a few TeV, so they are probably a small correction for the higgsino.

directions.goal: Use the serve-idm.sh tools to compute the pure-higgsino thermal relic density Omega h^2 at m_chi = 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 TeV, find the mass where Omega h^2 = 0.120, and run the combined constraint check at the thermal point.
directions.rationale: The task asks for relic densities computed with the inelastic-DM tools. Earlier directions d-01 and d-04 could only interpolate from one published point in 1411.6930 because no relic-density tool was connected at the time. compute_relic_density and check_all_constraints are now in the catalog, so this direction answers the core question directly. It also replaces the low-confidence m^2 rescaling (f-009, about 1.14 TeV) with tool output.
steps: Call describe_tools first. Record exactly what compute_relic_density includes: Sommerfeld enhancement, coannihilation with the charged state, the charged-neutral splitting (about 341-356 MeV), any delta_m dependence, and the Planck reference value. Note every parameter and its default.

Call compute_relic_density at m_chi = 900, 1000, 1100, 1200 and 1300 GeV with delta_m = 500 keV and the default charged splitting. Give each call a distinct label if the tool accepts one. Record Omega h^2 and the stated ratio to Planck.
If the tool exposes a Sommerfeld or coannihilation switch, repeat at 1000, 1100 and 1200 GeV with it toggled, so the size of the effect can be compared with 1411.6930 (0.127 versus 0.126).
Bracket the crossing Omega h^2 = 0.120 with at most 3 more evaluations between the two masses that straddle it, and report the thermal mass to about 10 GeV.
Sensitivity check: at the thermal mass, vary delta_m (about 400 and 600 keV) and, if exposed, the charged splitting (about 340 and 360 MeV). Report the change in Omega h^2.

Call check_all_constraints at the thermal mass with delta_m = 500 keV. Record the relic, LZ, Fermi-LAT and Planck CMB verdicts and the numbers the tool returns, including any LZ limit value at that mass.

Compare the tool's thermal mass with the 1411.6930 point (Omega h^2 = 0.126-0.127, mass inferred as 1172 GeV) and the f-009 estimate. State whether the tool's freeze-out treatment is perturbative or Sommerfeld-resummed.
success_criteria: Omega h^2 is reported from tool output (not interpolated) at all 5 masses, with the tool's physics assumptions stated.
A thermal mass is bracketed to within about 10 GeV and compared with 1411.6930 and f-009.
check_all_constraints is run at the thermal point, with each constraint verdict and its numbers quoted as returned.

directions.goal: Compute the inelastic Z-mediated recoil spectrum, the LZ event expectation and the (m_chi, delta_m) constraint map for the thermal higgsino. Reproduce or test the 2609.01590 preferred region (delta_m = 481-519 keV, m_chi = 1000-1183 GeV) against the 475 keV (IceCube) and 557 keV (Super-K + IceCube) neutrino lines.
directions.rationale: Inelastic scattering is the only direct-detection route for the higgsino at current exposures. There is an unresolved tension here. The hand calculation f-001 gives a kinematic delta_max of about 364-368 keV for v_max = 776 km/s. 2609.01590, however, fits delta_m of about 500 keV, which needs a high-velocity tail (from the LMC) or a different halo model. The tool calculation must settle what delta_m can still be reached, and under which halo assumptions.
steps: Call describe_tools (if not already returned in this session) to read the halo model, v_esc, v_E, form factor and exposure options for predict_recoil and scan_mass_splitting. Note whether an LMC or high-velocity-tail option exists.
Call predict_recoil at m_chi = 1100 GeV for delta_m = 300, 400, 480, 520 and 560 keV. Record E_R,min, v_min, the spectrum shape and the integrated rate above 100 keV.

Convert each rate into expected LZ events for 2.84 and 4.2 tonne-years, using the tool output if it provides the conversion, otherwise multiplying by the stated exposure. Compare with the single 248 keV event.

If the tool accepts v_esc or halo parameters, repeat the delta_m = 500 keV point with a raised v_esc (for example 600 km/s) or the high-velocity-tail option, to quantify how strongly the rate depends on the halo.

Run scan_mass_splitting over m_chi of about 900-1300 GeV and delta_m of about 300-650 keV. If the grid is large, call set_dispatch for a facility run; otherwise run it locally. Record which grid points pass each constraint, and record where the run executed exactly as the tool reports it.
Call plot_constraint_summary on the scan and plot_recoil_spectrum (inelastic versus elastic) at 1100 GeV and 500 keV. Report the returned PNG paths.
Call predict_annual_modulation at E_R of about 248 keV for delta_m = 500 keV, as a secondary signature.
Overlay or tabulate the 475 and 557 keV neutrino lines against the scan, and state whether any of the 2609.01590 region survives under the tool's halo model.
success_criteria: Tool-computed E_R,min, v_min and LZ expected events are reported for at least 4 delta_m values at 1.1 TeV and checked against f-001.
A scan in (m_chi, delta_m) is completed and plotted, with the execution site stated as reported.
A clear statement of whether delta_m of about 480-520 keV gives at least O(1) events under the tool's halo, and how the result changes with v_esc.

directions.goal: Close the remaining literature gaps: the 2205.04486 doublet thermal mass, the LZ 2024 and XENONnT SI limits near 1 TeV, and verbatim citations for Planck 2018 and Chen and Hill.
directions.rationale: The tool results from d-09 and d-10 need published benchmarks. The thermal mass needs a second independent calculation (q-08). The elastic comparison still rests on a linear extrapolation of the 40 GeV limit (f-008, f-011), and the Planck and Chen-Hill quotes are on the board but not yet in references.bib.
steps: download_arxiv_full_text for 2205.04486 and use read_arxiv_chunk to find the Y=1/2 doublet thermal mass and its uncertainty. Cite it verbatim.

Cite Planck 2018 (1807.06209, 'Omega_c h^2 = 0.120 +/- 0.001') and Chen and Hill (1912.07795, the 'less than 10^-48 cm^2 in the TeV mass regime' sentence) with the cite tool, using the files already downloaded in run 261016_110437.

Search 2410.17036.txt for a stated limit at high mass (for example 1 TeV or a scaling statement). If none is stated, use web_search only to find the LZ HEPData record or a paper that quotes the LZ 1 TeV limit, then read and cite the source.
Download 2303.14729 and search it for the high-mass XENONnT limit or a scaling statement. Cite any number found.
If budget remains, read the XLZD Design Book (2410.17137) for the neutrino-fog level and the projected sensitivity at about 1 TeV.
Tabulate predicted sigma_SI (at most 1e-48 cm^2) against the LZ, XENONnT and fog values at 1.1 TeV. Label each entry as read or extrapolated.
success_criteria: The 2205.04486 doublet thermal mass is quoted verbatim with its uncertainty.
references.bib contains the Planck, Chen-Hill and 2205.04486 entries with verbatim quotes.
At least one of the LZ or XENONnT 1 TeV limits is obtained from a citable source rather than extrapolated, or a dead end is recorded.

issues.text: The steps need about 17 calls: 1 describe, 5 masses, 3 toggles, up to 3 bracketing, 4 sensitivity, 1 constraint check. The budget is 15. Drop the 400 and 600 keV delta_m variations, since a keV-scale neutral splitting has a negligible effect on freeze-out. Keep one delta_m variation as a sanity check and use the 2 freed calls for the charged-splitting variations, which do matter through coannihilation.

If describe_tools shows that compute_relic_density is perturbative only, or omits coannihilation, the crossing will land near 1.0 TeV or lower. It must then not be reported as the higgsino thermal mass. State the result as tool output under those stated assumptions, and compare it with 1411.6930 and 2205.04486 (from d-11) rather than replacing them.

The 1172 GeV value for 1411.6930 is inferred, not stated in the paper. Label it as inferred everywhere. For check_all_constraints, record whether its LZ test is elastic SI, inelastic, or both, and which exposure it assumes. Without this, the LZ verdict cannot be interpreted.

Do not call set_dispatch to polaris or perlmutter. No IRI or Globus authentication has been established, and get_dispatch reports local execution. Size the grid so it runs locally, for example 5 masses by 8 delta_m values, and report the site as returned.

Event counts are unverifiable without LZ signal efficiency and the analysis region of interest near 248 keV, since the standard WIMP search region ends well below that. State the acceptance the tool uses. If the tool has none, report counts as 100 percent acceptance upper bounds and label them that way.

f-001 checks out: mu of about 110 GeV and v of 776 km/s give delta_max of about 368 keV. A standard halo therefore gives zero events at 480-520 keV, and the result rests entirely on halo assumptions. Make the v_esc or high-velocity-tail variation mandatory, not conditional. If the tool has no such knob, record that it cannot test 2609.01590 and stop rather than reporting zero events as a refutation. The 475 and 557 keV lines are literature values, not tool output. Label them as such, and note that the 557 keV line excludes the whole 481-519 keV window.
Annual modulation at 248 keV near the kinematic edge is a low-priority call. Drop it if the budget is tight. Skip the extra check_all_constraints call because d-09 already covers it.
The files from run 261016_110437 may not persist. Run list_files on downloads first, and budget re-downloads if they are missing. Confirm 2205.04486 with get_arxiv_metadata before citing it.

The higgsino SI prediction carries a large theoretical uncertainty from Higgs and gauge-loop cancellation, so 'at most 1e-48' is not a central value. Quote the Chen and Hill band with its uncertainty. A linear high-mass extrapolation of the LZ limit is acceptable if it is labeled, but the extrapolation formula must be stated.

open questions of particle physics and cosmology. Weakly

most studied candidates, since masses and interactions

TeV, reproduce the observed relic abundance and provide
concrete targets for direct, indirect, and collider searches

of this mass range.

248±23 stat±23 sys keVnr and has a local significance
of about 3.4σand a global significance of 2.6σ[3]. This
event is kinematically compatible with TeV-scale DM,
though standard elastic scenarios are disfavored by null

the Fermi-LAT excess is a broad spectral component at

strained at the highest energies. A TeV-scale WIMP an-
nihilating into gauge-boson and Higgs-boson pairs pro-

The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) collaboration has recently reported a single nuclear recoil event at a high
recoil energy of about 250 keV. This has been interpreted as inelastic scattering of dark matter that
is a supersymmetric Higgsino with a mass splitting between the neutral states of a few 100 keV.
Such dark matter may be captured at high recoil in the Sun through scattering on heavy elements
in it, and annihilate to W +W − and ZZ , in turn giving rise to a neutrino flux detectable on Earth.
Using measurements of atmospheric electron- and muon-neutrino fluxes by Super-Kamiokande and
IceCube, we constrain thermal and non-thermal Higgsino dark matter, excluding inter-state mass
splittings ≲ 557 keV. This disfavors Higgsino-like interpretations of the LZ event for standard halo

I. INTRODUCTION
The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, seeking direct de-
tection of dark matter (DM), has seen a 248 ± 23 (stat)
± 23 (sys) keV nuclear recoil energy event, LZ230616, in
its 2.84 tonne-year dataset at a global (local) significance
of 2.6σ (3.4σ) [1]. The collaboration interpreted this as

The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) collaboration has recently reported a single nuclear recoil event at a high
recoil energy of about 250 keV. This has been interpreted as inelastic scattering of dark matter that
is a supersymmetric Higgsino with a mass splitting between the neutral states of a few 100 keV.
Such dark matter may be captured at high recoil in the Sun through scattering on heavy elements
in it, and annihilate to W +W − and ZZ , in turn giving rise to a neutrino flux detectable on Earth.
Using measurements of atmospheric electron- and muon-neutrino fluxes by Super-Kamiokande and
IceCube, we constrain thermal and non-thermal Higgsino dark matter, excluding inter-state mass
splittings ≲ 557 keV. This disfavors Higgsino-like interpretations of the LZ event for standard halo
velocities.

I. INTRODUCTION
The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, seeking direct de-
tection of dark matter (DM), has seen a 248 ± 23 (stat)
± 23 (sys) keV nuclear recoil energy event, LZ230616, in
its 2.84 tonne-year dataset at a global (local) significance
of 2.6σ (3.4σ) [1]. The collaboration interpreted this as
induced by effective operators that lead to momentum-
dependent elastic scattering (via a magnetic moment)
or endothermic inelastic scattering; other operators such
as scalar-scalar interactions would have produced events
at low recoils that were not observed. One particularly
attractive explanation of LZ230616 [ 2–7] is, with an in-
elastic mass splitting δ≃ 350 keV, the thermal Higgsino,
a 1.08 TeV mass supersymmetric partner of the Higgs
boson – arising in weak-scale supersymmetric extensions
of the Standard Model (SM) [8–10] – that freezes out to
the right DM abundance via co-annihilations with slightly
heavier neutral and charged Higgsino states, dubbed the
“last-standing electroweak WIMP” and a poster child
for electroweak multiplets in the so-called minimal DM
paradigm [11]. Such Higgsino-like dark matter is accessi-
ble at collider energies, is being sought in indirect searches
for its annihilation products [ 12–15], and possibly large
δs may be cornered in compact stars [16–21].
While the thermal Higgsino DM interpretation is in
slight tension with a lack of events in LZ’s high-energy
sideband [23, 24] (which could be tested in LZ’s upcoming
runs and relaxed by considering a lighter non-thermal
Higgsino DM), a more urgent tension has been pointed
out. The 1.08 TeV Higgsino DM can be captured in
the Sun for δ <566 keV by scattering on its constituent
heavy elements, e.g., lead, thermalize within the solar
core, and subsequently annihilate to W +W−/ ZZ giving
rise to a high-energy neutrino flux that is constrained by

IV. RESUL TS
In Fig. 2 we show for thermal Higgsino DM our limits,
as well as a band enclosing δ = 340− 360 keV preferred
by LZ230616. The slope of these limits can be understood
from the tree-level vs loop-level scattering of χ. For
the heaviest solar nuclei, tree-level inelastic scattering is
suppressed due to kinematic threshold when χ reaches a
radius∼ 0.2R⊙ after losing kinetic energy via repeated
scatters. If the loop-level SI and SD cross sections are
then large enough, χ can scatter further and settle into
smaller volumes within the Sun, which would enhance its
annihilation rates. This is reflected in Fig. 2, where for SI
(SD) cross sections up to ∼ 2× 10−52 cm2 (∼ 2× 10−48
cm2) loop-level elastic scattering is inefficient for the
thermalization of χ, and the limit on δ is flat. As these
cross sections are increased, rχ shrinks and saturates to

--- Page 5 ---
5
rth, where the limit on δ flattens again.
The hierarchy of our limits is understood from detector
sizes, energy thresholds, and angular resolutions. The
1.08 TeV thermal Higgsino produces a broad neutrino
spectrum in the Sun. With its higher energy threshold
than Super-K, IceCube probes the harder part of the
spectrum, containing a significant fraction of the signal
flux. However, this flux is rapidly falling with energy,
hence the smaller detector of Super-K registers much
fewer events – though thanks to its lower threshold it can
access the softer part of the signal spectrum that IceCube
cannot reach. Together, these effects make Super-K limits
weaker than those from IceCube. Further, IceCube – νµ
measurements benefit from a significantly better angular
resolution than the νe cascade observations, explaining
its slightly stronger limits. Now between the Super-K
datasets, although the atmospheric νµ flux is smaller
than that of νes, the νe data is only provided up to 100
GeV while νµ measurements extend to higher energies,
making the Super-K–νµ limits stronger. Note that our
strongest (IceCube –νµ) and weakest (Super-K –νe) limits
on δ differ by only∼ 20% despite various uncertainties
in instrumental systematics and atmospheric neutrino
models. Our limits overall are competitive with those
obtained from the IceCube 2025 dataset by Ref. [25].

Our results show that high-energy νe and νµ measure-
ments at IceCube and Super-K disfavor the Higgsino inter-
pretation of the anomalous LZ230616 event. Our results
complement Ref. [25], which used the latest IceCube mea-
surements of νµs from the solar direction. We have also
ruled out a significant parametric region of a non-thermal
Higgsino DM interpretation of LZ230616. Future observa-
tions by upcoming telescopes such as Hyper-Kamiokande
and KM3NeT can further improve these bounds and
potentially discover the existence of a (non-)thermal Hig-
gsino – as could direct detectors such as LZ, XENONnT,
and PandaX-4T.
We re-state that our results do not completely rule

tidal streams [54–56]. Moreover, for ∼250 keV recoils of

Conclusions.We have investigated a thermal higgsino
interpretation of the LZ high-energy recoil and the Fermi-
LAT Galactic-center preference. Thermal freeze-out fixes
the higgsino mass near 1.1 TeV, while the LZ recoil se-
lects the neutral-state splitting through the high-velocity
tail of the local dark-matter distribution. With the LMC-
enhanced Halo 13 distribution, the joint 1σregion gives
481≲δ m/keV≲519. Solar-neutrino searches provide
a decisive complementary test. A thermalizing captured
population requiresδ m ≳553 keV, outside the LZ 2σre-
gions. Near the blind spot of elastic scattering, however,
the captured higgsinos remain on extended nonthermal
orbits, lowering the IceCube boundary to 475 keV, or to
466 keV with the loose solar and nuclear inputs. The full
Halo 13 LZ 2σinterval can therefore remain compatible
with IceCube when the residual elastic scattering is neg-
ligible. The same region predicts a Galactic-center line
and endpoint signal close to the present H.E.S.S. limits
and within the projected reach of CTAO, providing a
direct test of this interpretation.
Note added.Ref. [43] pointed out that the higgsino
interpretation of the LZ event can predict additional nu-
clear recoils in the high-energy sideband. For the Halo 13
MW+LMC, the smallest mass splittingδ m = 475 keV
givesN raw

therefore provides an important additional test of this
scenario, but does not by itself establish an exclusion

Conclusions.We have investigated a thermal higgsino
interpretation of the LZ high-energy recoil and the Fermi-
LAT Galactic-center preference. Thermal freeze-out fixes
the higgsino mass near 1.1 TeV, while the LZ recoil se-
lects the neutral-state splitting through the high-velocity
tail of the local dark-matter distribution. With the LMC-
enhanced Halo 13 distribution, the joint 1σregion gives
481≲δ m/keV≲519. Solar-neutrino searches provide
a decisive complementary test. A thermalizing captured
population requiresδ m ≳553 keV, outside the LZ 2σre-
gions. Near the blind spot of elastic scattering, however,
the captured higgsinos remain on extended nonthermal
orbits, lowering the IceCube boundary to 475 keV, or to
466 keV with the loose solar and nuclear inputs. The full
Halo 13 LZ 2σinterval can therefore remain compatible
with IceCube when the residual elastic scattering is neg-
ligible. The same region predicts a Galactic-center line
and endpoint signal close to the present H.E.S.S. limits
and within the projected reach of CTAO, providing a
direct test of this interpretation.
Note added.Ref. [43] pointed out that the higgsino
interpretation of the LZ event can predict additional nu-
clear recoils in the high-energy sideband. For the Halo 13
MW+LMC, the smallest mass splittingδ m = 475 keV
givesN raw
SB /NROI ≃3.39. The high-energy sideband
therefore provides an important additional test of this
scenario, but does not by itself establish an exclusion
without the corresponding detector acceptance.

We re-state that our results do not completely rule
out the thermal Higgsino interpretation of LZ230616. It
could remain viable if the local DM velocity distribution
receives non-standard contributions such as from the mo-
tion of the LMC [ 2] or unvirialized substructure, e.g.,
tidal streams [54–56]. Moreover, for ∼250 keV recoils of
xenon the Helm form factor is in a region where it rapidly
oscillates with ER, so that its use may not be robust.
With numerous models being proposed involving in-
elastic scatters explaining LZ230616 [ 5, 57–67] and hints
of other high-recoil events fitted with inelastic and
momentum-dependent elastic operators [ 68], these are
exciting times for the dark matter hunter!

IV. RESUL TS
In Fig. 2 we show for thermal Higgsino DM our limits,
as well as a band enclosing δ = 340− 360 keV preferred
by LZ230616. The slope of these limits can be understood
from the tree-level vs loop-level scattering of χ. For
the heaviest solar nuclei, tree-level inelastic scattering is
suppressed due to kinematic threshold when χ reaches a
radius∼ 0.2R⊙ after losing kinetic energy via repeated
scatters. If the loop-level SI and SD cross sections are
then large enough, χ can scatter further and settle into
smaller volumes within the Sun, which would enhance its
annihilation rates. This is reflected in Fig. 2, where for SI
(SD) cross sections up to ∼ 2× 10−52 cm2 (∼ 2× 10−48
cm2) loop-level elastic scattering is inefficient for the
thermalization of χ, and the limit on δ is flat. As these
cross sections are increased, rχ shrinks and saturates to

--- Page 5 ---
5
rth, where the limit on δ flattens again.
The hierarchy of our limits is understood from detector
sizes, energy thresholds, and angular resolutions. The
1.08 TeV thermal Higgsino produces a broad neutrino
spectrum in the Sun. With its higher energy threshold
than Super-K, IceCube probes the harder part of the
spectrum, containing a significant fraction of the signal
flux. However, this flux is rapidly falling with energy,
hence the smaller detector of Super-K registers much
fewer events – though thanks to its lower threshold it can
access the softer part of the signal spectrum that IceCube
cannot reach. Together, these effects make Super-K limits
weaker than those from IceCube. Further, IceCube – νµ
measurements benefit from a significantly better angular
resolution than the νe cascade observations, explaining
its slightly stronger limits. Now between the Super-K
datasets, although the atmospheric νµ flux is smaller
than that of νes, the νe data is only provided up to 100
GeV while νµ measurements extend to higher energies,
making the Super-K–νµ limits stronger. Note that our
strongest (IceCube –νµ) and weakest (Super-K –νe) limits
on δ differ by only∼ 20% despite various uncertainties
in instrumental systematics and atmospheric neutrino
models. Our limits overall are competitive with those
obtained from the IceCube 2025 dataset by Ref. [25].
In Fig. 3 we show our limits on the non-thermal Hig-
gsino by varying mχ, also adding a recast of IceCube – νµ
[2025] [26] data for an indirect comparison with Ref. [ 25]
(which only considered a thermal Higgsino). For the re-
cast, we use the limits in Ref. [ 26] (provided up to mχ =
104 GeV) and scale it by the SI capture rate in Ref. [38] to
obtain the limits on the DM annihilation rate, Γ ann. The
hierarchy of limits follow that of Fig. 2; our benchmarks
σloop
SI = 0 (σloop
SI = 10−48 cm2) are representative of all
loop-level SI cross sections above (below) σSI∼ 10−50
cm2 that saturate the upper limit on δ as seen in Fig. 2.
For sub-TeV masses we see that the limits from IceCube
are weakening, which is due to its steep energy threshold,

arXiv ID: 2610.03692
Title: Higgsino dark matter compatible with the LUX-ZEPLIN high-energy nuclear-recoil event and IceCube constraints
Authors: Katherine Freese, Dionysios P. Theodosopoulos
Year: 2026
Abstract: We examine Higgsino dark matter (DM) as a potential explanation of the $248~\mathrm{keV}$ nuclear-recoil event of interest reported by the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, taking into account IceCube constraints on DM annihilation in the Sun. In the nearly pure Higgsino limit, two neutral Majorana states separated by a small mass splitting $δ$ are connected by an off-diagonal coupling to the $Z$ boson, providing a natural realization of inelastic DM. Using a likelihood analysis, we identify 90\% confidence regions compatible with the LZ event and consistent with the null results of IceCube searches, both with and without including a constraint from the absence of events in the LZ high-energy sideband. In our LZ analysis, we consider the DM distribution in the Standard Halo Model alone as well as possible enhancements of the high-speed tail induced by the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). We present four variants of bounds from IceCube on Higgsino dark matter, depending on various assumptions on cooling channels in the Sun, motivated by severe theoretical uncertainties about Higgsino-nucleon elastic scattering (unimportant for direct detection but crucial for IceCube bounds). Whereas the thermal Higgsino with a mass of $1.1~\mathrm{TeV}$ remains only marginally compatible with both the LZ event and the IceCube limits when the LMC-induced high-speed tail is included and both elastic cooling in the Sun and the LZ high-energy sideband constraint are neglected, higher mass Higgsinos are excellent candidates for the LZ event in light of IceCube constraints. Depending on the halo distribution, cooling interactions, and whether the LZ high-energy sideband is included, the compatible regions in the Higgsino parameter space $(m_χ,δ)$ extend from masses of $\sim2~\mathrm{TeV}$ to hundreds of TeV or higher, with mass splittings ranging approximately from $350$ to $525~\mathrm{keV}$.

arXiv ID: 2609.09830
Title: Radiative Corrections to the Direct Detection of Inelastic Scattering of Higgsino-like Neutralino Dark Matter
Authors: Arindam Chatterjee, Debottam Das, Syed Adil Pasha, Alexander Pukhov, Rahul Puri
Year: 2026
Abstract: The direct detection (DD) of Higgsino-like dark matter (DM) through inelastic scattering processes may provide a promising avenue, along with the elastic scattering, when the mass splitting between the neutral Higgsino pairs is extremely tiny. The mass splitting can be reduced further by adopting the on-shell renormalization for the neutral and charged Higgsinos in the MSSM. Moreover, all the one-loop electroweak (EW) corrections to the three-point vertices for the neutralino(s)-Higgs interactions have been considered, while both elastic and inelastic DM-nucleon scattering cross-sections have been calculated primarily through Higgs exchange. Subsequently, the expected number of scattering events in the latest LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) DD experiment are also computed. Our results highlight a few scenarios in which the inelastic component may exceed the corresponding elastic component, leading to enhanced direct detection scattering rates.

arXiv ID: 2609.06890
Title: High-Energy Nuclear Recoils from Boosted Dark Matter for the LZ 248-keV Event: Beyond the Halo-Dependent High-Velocity Tail
Authors: Haider Alhazmi, Doojin Kim, Kyoungchul Kong, Jong-Chul Park, Seodong Shin
Year: 2026
Abstract: The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Collaboration has reported a nuclear-recoil candidate at $E_R=248\pm23_{\rm stat}\pm23_{\rm sys}$ keV, with a maximum local significance of $3.4σ$ and a global significance of $2.6σ$. A prominent interpretation invokes heavy halo dark matter near an inelastic threshold and therefore depends sensitively on the poorly constrained high-speed tail of the Galactic velocity distribution. In this Letter, we propose a qualitatively different possibility based on light boosted dark matter (BDM), whose incident energy is determined primarily by the dark-sector mass spectrum. We consider multi-component scenarios in which the boosted state scatters elastically or inelastically off xenon nuclei. For elastic scattering, pseudoscalar-mediated momentum dependence suppresses low-energy recoils. Near-threshold endothermic scattering of a nearly monochromatic BDM flux can instead confine the signal between kinematically determined recoil endpoints, suppressing events in both the low- and high-energy sidebands. The upscattered state may furthermore decay invisibly within the dark sector, preserving a single-nuclear-recoil signature without requiring it to be detector-stable. We present representative benchmark spectra and discuss complementary tests using other target nuclei and large-volume liquid-scintillator experiments.

delta: **Completed — Use the serve-idm.sh tools to compute the pure-higgsino thermal relic density Omega h^2 at m_chi = 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 TeV, find the mass where Omega h^2 = 0.120, and run the combined constraint check at the thermal point..** Done. compute_relic_density (serve-idm.sh) gives Omega h^2 = 0.0731, 0.0898, 0.1083, 0.1285 and 0.1503 at m_chi = 900, 1000, 1100, 1200 and 1300 GeV. It gives 0.1181 at 1150 GeV and 0.1202 at 1160 GeV, so the thermal mass (Omega h^2 = 0.120, Planck 0.12 +/- 0.0012) is about 1159 GeV, bracketed between 1150 and 1160 GeV (f-020). This is about 1 percent below the 1172 GeV inferred from 1411.6930 and about 2 percent above the f-009 estimate of about 1.14 TeV. The agreement is by construction, not from independent physics. The tool does perturbative Kolb-Turner freeze-out (x_f about 24.5, g* = 86.25) with sigma_v = 2.5e-26 cm^3/s x (1100 GeV/m_chi)^2. It has no Sommerfeld or coannihilation switch, no charged-splitting input and no delta_m dependence: Omega h^2 = 0.1202 at delta = 400, 500 and 600 keV (f-021). So step 3 (toggling Sommerfeld/coannihilation) and the charged-splitting part of step 5 could not be run. The tool's consistent_planck flag is unreliable: it reads True at 25 sigma tension and False at 39 sigma. check_all_constraints at 1160 GeV, delta = 500 keV returns 'VIABLE'. Relic is 0.1202 (0.1 sigma). LZ gives N_expected = 0.00 for 2.84 t-yr with sigma_n = 7.43e-39 cm^2, flagged inconsistent with the 1 observed event; no LZ limit value is returned. Fermi-LAT: sigma_v_today = 1.04e-41 cm^3/s against a limit of 2.48e-25. CMB: p_ann = 1.35e-45 against a limit of 3.2e-28. Results at 400 and 600 keV are similar (f-022). Warning: the tool treats annihilation today as p-wave and splitting-suppressed, at odds with the s-wave higgsino WW/ZZ rate of about 1e-26 cm^3/s, so its indirect and CMB passes are not physically reliable (q-15). No files or figures were produced.

**Completed — Compute the inelastic Z-mediated recoil spectrum, the LZ event expectation and the (m_chi, delta_m) constraint map for the thermal higgsino. Reproduce or test the 2609.01590 preferred region (delta_m = 481-519 keV, m_chi = 1000-1183 GeV) against the 475 keV (IceCube) and 557 keV (Super-K + IceCube) neutrino lines..** All runs were local; get_dispatch reported 'local execution'. The tool uses a standard halo with a hard cutoff at v_esc+v_E = 776 km/s, and none of its calls accept a v_esc or LMC-tail option. At m_chi = 1100 GeV (sigma_n = 7.43e-39 cm^2), predict_recoil gives these values for delta = 300/400/480/520/560 keV: peak E_R = 270/360/432/468/504 keV, v_min at the peak = 701/809/886/922/957 km/s, and v_min at 248 keV = 701/823/921/969/1018 km/s. Expected events in the LZ extended nuclear-recoil search (2.84 t-yr): 744.6 at 300 keV and 0.00 for every delta of 400 keV or more. Scaling by exposure gives about 1101 events at 4.2 t-yr for 300 keV, and still zero for the rest. The tool reports only the peak E_R, not a separate E_R,min, and gives no integrated rate above 100 keV. These results agree with f-001's kinematic limit of about 365 keV (f-018). At (1100 GeV, 500 keV), check_all_constraints gives Omega h^2 = 0.108 and N_LZ = 0, marked 'not consistent with 1 event'. Fermi and CMB pass by many orders of magnitude, and the annual modulation at 248 keV is zero. The 15x15 scan (m_chi 900-1300 GeV, delta 300-650 keV, file /Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/scan_idm.npz) finds 180 of 225 points pass all constraints, but only 12 predict 0.3-5 LZ events. Its best fit is m_chi = 986 GeV, delta = 350 keV, which lies below both the 475 keV (IceCube) and 557 keV (Super-K + IceCube) neutrino lines (f-019, f-023). The scan output does not list which points are in the 12-point group, so the claim that they all sit below the neutrino lines is inferred from the 1.1 TeV kinematics, not confirmed by the tool. Plots: constraint summary at /Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/constraint_summary.png and the 1100 GeV / 500 keV recoil spectrum at /Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/recoil_spectrum.png; the tools return no figure numbers. Conclusion: under the tool's halo, delta of about 480-520 keV gives zero events, not O(1), so no part of the 2609.01590 region survives. Explaining the LZ event at about 500 keV needs a high-velocity tail (for example from the LMC), which the tool does not model. How the rate changes with v_esc could not be tested, because no tool exposes halo parameters (dead end x-03).

args.claim: The 475 keV and 557 keV neutrino lines differ because of how the captured population in the Sun is treated, not because of the halo. 2609.01590 simulates a non-thermal population on extended solar orbits at m_chi = 1.11 TeV with no elastic cooling (elastic blind spot) and 10-year IceCube data, using <sigma v>_eff of about 1.5e-26 cm^3/s with Sommerfeld; this gives delta_m >~ 475 keV excluded at 90% CL (466 keV with loose solar/nuclear inputs, about 454 keV with the Fe nuclear-response uncertainty). If elastic scattering allows thermalization and capture-annihilation equilibrium, the same paper gets delta_m >~ 553 keV. 2609.07807 assumes thermalization within the Sun after capture, a standard truncated Maxwellian (u0 = 220 km/s, v_esc = 544 km/s, v_sun = 232 km/s), rho = 0.4 GeV/cm^3, sigma_chi_n = 7.4e-39 cm^2, <sigma v> = 1.3e-26 cm^3/s, m_chi = 1.08 TeV and a 95% CL chi^2 on IceCube nu_mu (2016), IceCube nu_e and Super-K data. It excludes delta_m <~ 557 keV and states the interpretation could remain viable with an LMC tail or substructure.
args.note: Fig. 2 of 2609.01590 and Figs. 2-3 of 2609.07807. The 557 keV limit is flat for loop SI below about 2e-52 cm^2 and loop SD below about 2e-48 cm^2. The equilibrium result of 2609.01590 (553 keV) agrees with 557 keV.

delta:
**Completed — Extract verbatim, citable inputs from the 2026 LZ-event papers: the halo models, rates and preferred regions, the neutrino exclusion lines, the radiative corrections and the rescue scenarios..** I read the full texts of 2609.01590 and 2609.07807 and only the abstracts of 2610.03692, 2609.09830 and 2609.06890. The validated citations are in /Users/nramachandra/hep-genesis-testing/projects/ramp-research-higgsino-dd/runs/261022_110244/references.bib (keys arxiv260901590 and arxiv260907807). Not every number has a validated quote: the cite tool rejected several 2609.01590 sentences (the v_esc + v_E endpoint sentence, the 0.815-0.900 H.E.S.S. ratio, the 553 keV equilibrium bound, the Maxwellian best fit and the relic mass ranges) because the PDF text garbles math symbols and en-dash ranges. Those numbers were read directly in the text (tc-...-32, -36, -44) but have no validated quote (dead end x-04).

1. Preferred region, 2609.01590 (f-024, Fig. 1). With the Halo 13 MW+LMC velocity distribution the LZ fit gives delta_m = 481-519 keV at 1 sigma and 475-529 keV at 2 sigma, best fit about 496 keV. With a profiled Maxwellian halo it gives 312-422 keV at 1 sigma and 280-457 keV at 2 sigma, best fit 1.09 TeV and 366 keV. The paper says the upper limit on delta_m is set by the kinematic endpoint v_esc + v_E, not by the event-rate normalization. The relic density fixes m_chi = 1000-1183 GeV at 1 sigma and 943-1230 GeV at 2 sigma. LZ inputs are E_R = 248 +/- 23 stat +/- 23 sys keV and 2.84 tonne-year.

2. Why the neutrino lines are 475 and 557 keV (f-025; Fig. 2 of 2609.01590, Figs. 2-3 of 2609.07807). The difference comes from how the captured higgsinos are treated in the Sun, not from the halo model.
- 2609.01590, at m_chi = 1.11 TeV: if elastic scattering is negligible (the blind spot), the captured higgsinos never thermalize and stay on extended orbits, so they annihilate less. With <sigma v>_eff of about 1.5e-26 cm^3/s and ten years of IceCube data, this excludes delta_m up to about 475 keV at 90% CL. Loose solar and nuclear inputs lower this to 466 keV, and the Fe nuclear-response uncertainty to about 454 keV. If elastic scattering lets them reach equilibrium, the same paper finds delta_m >~ 553 keV.
- 2609.07807 assumes the captured higgsinos thermalize and uses a standard truncated Maxwellian halo: u0 = 220 km/s, v_esc = 544 km/s, v_sun = 232 km/s, rho = 0.4 GeV/cm^3. Other inputs are sigma_chi_n = 7.4e-39 cm^2, <sigma v> = 1.3e-26 cm^3/s and m_chi = 1.08 TeV, with a 95% CL fit to IceCube nu_mu, IceCube nu_e and Super-K data. It excludes delta_m below about 557 keV, which agrees with the 553 keV equilibrium result. It still allows rescue by an LMC tail or substructure.

3. Gamma-ray lines near 1.1 TeV, 2609.01590 (f-026, Fig. 3). The thermal prediction is 0.815-0.900 of the H.E.S.S. 546 h limits, which the paper calls close to, but not excluded by, the present limits. The CTAO Alpha 500 h projection, mu_gamma,95 = 1.69, falls short of the thermal target. The Omega configuration, estimated at 0.85, would reach it. Dwarf-galaxy, CMB and ATLAS disappearing-track limits do not exclude the region.

4. Rescue and alternative scenarios, abstracts only (f-027).
- 2610.03692: the 1.1 TeV thermal higgsino is only marginally compatible with the LZ event and IceCube, and only with the LMC tail, no elastic cooling in the Sun and no sideband constraint. Compatible regions run from about 2 TeV to hundreds of TeV, with delta about 350-525 keV.
- 2609.09830: one-loop electroweak corrections with on-shell renormalization reduce delta_m. The abstract gives no size for the change.
- 2609.06890: light boosted dark matter, which does not depend on the halo velocity tail.

Still open (q-16): how large the 2609.09830 radiative correction is, and the numbers for the four IceCube variants in 2610.03692.

issues.text: The central task question has not been answered quantitatively: where does the elastic SI cross section of the thermal higgsino sit relative to the LZ 4.2 t-yr and XENONnT 90% CL curves at 1.0-1.2 TeV? No finding gives either the higgsino SI value (loop and Higgs-mediated, around 1e-48 to 1e-49 cm^2 with possible cancellation) or the limit values at 1.1 TeV. d-11 is still open, and this comparison is the core of the headline answer.

The thermal mass of about 1159 GeV is set by the tool's hard-coded normalization (sigma_v = 2.5e-26 x (1100/m)^2). It is a calibration, not a computation. The report must not present it as an independent check of 1411.6930. The Sommerfeld/coannihilation step and the charged-splitting sensitivity in the brief were never done. A literature or analytic estimate (1008.2905 method) is needed if the task's 'with and without Sommerfeld' item is to be answered.

The tool's indirect-detection and CMB passes rest on a p-wave, splitting-suppressed annihilation today. This is unphysical for a higgsino, which annihilates s-wave to WW/ZZ at about 1-1.5e-26 cm^3/s. The 'VIABLE' label for indirect and CMB constraints should be replaced by a comparison of the s-wave rate with the Fermi dwarf and H.E.S.S. continuum and line limits at 1.1 TeV, together with f-026.

The claim that no LZ-reproducing point survives the neutrino limits is inferred from the 1.1 TeV kinematics and the single best fit. The 12 'best_fit_region' points were never listed. The npz file exists and should be loaded to confirm their (m_chi, delta) values. A second point needs checking: the tool gives zero events at 400 keV, while the profiled Maxwellian in 2609.01590 reaches 422 keV (1 sigma) and 457 keV (2 sigma). Either the tool's v_max = 776 km/s is lower than the profiled v_esc, or the treatments differ. This should be reconciled analytically.

Several headline literature numbers rest on text that was read but has no validated quote (x-04). Re-fetching narrower character windows around the relevant passages would let the excerpts carry the values even if the cite tool continues to reject garbled math.

Earlier directions d-01 and d-04 could only interpolate from one published point in 1411.6930 because no relic-density tool was connected at the time. compute_relic_density and check_all_constraints are now in the catalog, so this direction answers the core question directly. steps: Call describe_tools first. Record exactly what compute_relic_density includes: Sommerfeld enhancement, coannihilation with the charged state, the charged-neutral splitting (about 341-356 MeV), any delta_m dependence, and the Planck reference value. Note every parameter and its default.

result.summary: Done. compute_relic_density (serve-idm.sh) gives Omega h^2 = 0.0731, 0.0898, 0.1083, 0.1285 and 0.1503 at m_chi = 900, 1000, 1100, 1200 and 1300 GeV. It gives 0.1181 at 1150 GeV and 0.1202 at 1160 GeV, so the thermal mass (Omega h^2 = 0.120, Planck 0.12 +/- 0.0012) is about 1159 GeV, bracketed between 1150 and 1160 GeV (f-020). This is about 1 percent below the 1172 GeV inferred from 1411.6930 and about 2 percent above the f-009 estimate of about 1.14 TeV. The agreement is by construction, not from independent physics. The tool does perturbative Kolb-Turner freeze-out (x_f about 24.5, g* = 86.25) with sigma_v = 2.5e-26 cm^3/s x (1100 GeV/m_chi)^2. It has no Sommerfeld or coannihilation switch, no charged-splitting input and no delta_m dependence: Omega h^2 = 0.1202 at delta = 400, 500 and 600 keV (f-021). So step 3 (toggling Sommerfeld/coannihilation) and the charged-splitting part of step 5 could not be run. The tool's consistent_planck flag is unreliable: it reads True at 25 sigma tension and False at 39 sigma. check_all_constraints at 1160 GeV, delta = 500 keV returns 'VIABLE'. Relic is 0.1202 (0.1 sigma). LZ gives N_expected = 0.00 for 2.84 t-yr with sigma_n = 7.43e-39 cm^2, flagged inconsistent with the 1 observed event; no LZ limit value is returned. Fermi-LAT: sigma_v_today = 1.04e-41 cm^3/s against a limit of 2.48e-25. CMB: p_ann = 1.35e-45 against a limit of 3.2e-28. Results at 400 and 600 keV are similar (f-022). Warning: the tool treats annihilation today as p-wave and splitting-suppressed, at odds with the s-wave higgsino WW/ZZ rate of about 1e-26 cm^3/s, so its indirect and CMB passes are not physically reliable (q-15). No files or figures were produced.

result.summary: All runs were local; get_dispatch reported 'local execution'. The tool uses a standard halo with a hard cutoff at v_esc+v_E = 776 km/s, and none of its calls accept a v_esc or LMC-tail option. At m_chi = 1100 GeV (sigma_n = 7.43e-39 cm^2), predict_recoil gives these values for delta = 300/400/480/520/560 keV: peak E_R = 270/360/432/468/504 keV, v_min at the peak = 701/809/886/922/957 km/s, and v_min at 248 keV = 701/823/921/969/1018 km/s. Expected events in the LZ extended nuclear-recoil search (2.84 t-yr): 744.6 at 300 keV and 0.00 for every delta of 400 keV or more. Scaling by exposure gives about 1101 events at 4.2 t-yr for 300 keV, and still zero for the rest. The tool reports only the peak E_R, not a separate E_R,min, and gives no integrated rate above 100 keV. These results agree with f-001's kinematic limit of about 365 keV (f-018). At (1100 GeV, 500 keV), check_all_constraints gives Omega h^2 = 0.108 and N_LZ = 0, marked 'not consistent with 1 event'. Fermi and CMB pass by many orders of magnitude, and the annual modulation at 248 keV is zero. The 15x15 scan (m_chi 900-1300 GeV, delta 300-650 keV, file /Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/scan_idm.npz) finds 180 of 225 points pass all constraints, but only 12 predict 0.3-5 LZ events. Its best fit is m_chi = 986 GeV, delta = 350 keV, which lies below both the 475 keV (IceCube) and 557 keV (Super-K + IceCube) neutrino lines (f-019, f-023). The scan output does not list which points are in the 12-point group, so the claim that they all sit below the neutrino lines is inferred from the 1.1 TeV kinematics, not confirmed by the tool. Plots: constraint summary at /Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/constraint_summary.png and the 1100 GeV / 500 keV recoil spectrum at /Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/recoil_spectrum.png; the tools return no figure numbers. Conclusion: under the tool's halo, delta of about 480-520 keV gives zero events, not O(1), so no part of the 2609.01590 region survives. Explaining the LZ event at about 500 keV needs a high-velocity tail (for example from the LMC), which the tool does not model. How the rate changes with v_esc could not be tested, because no tool exposes halo parameters (dead end x-03).

I read the full texts of 2609.01590 and 2609.07807 and only the abstracts of 2610.03692, 2609.09830 and 2609.06890. The validated citations are in /Users/nramachandra/hep-genesis-testing/projects/ramp-research-higgsino-dd/runs/261022_110244/references.bib (keys arxiv260901590 and arxiv260907807). Not every number has a validated quote: the cite tool rejected several 2609.01590 sentences (the v_esc + v_E endpoint sentence, the 0.815-0.900 H.E.S.S. ratio, the 553 keV equilibrium bound, the Maxwellian best fit and the relic mass ranges) because the PDF text garbles math symbols and en-dash ranges. Those numbers were read directly in the text (tc-...-32, -36, -44) but have no validated quote (dead end x-04).

1. Preferred region, 2609.01590 (f-024, Fig. 1). With the Halo 13 MW+LMC velocity distribution the LZ fit gives delta_m = 481-519 keV at 1 sigma and 475-529 keV at 2 sigma, best fit about 496 keV. With a profiled Maxwellian halo it gives 312-422 keV at 1 sigma and 280-457 keV at 2 sigma, best fit 1.09 TeV and 366 keV. The paper says the upper limit on delta_m is set by the kinematic endpoint v_esc + v_E, not by the event-rate normalization. The relic density fixes m_chi = 1000-1183 GeV at 1 sigma and 943-1230 GeV at 2 sigma. LZ inputs are E_R = 248 +/- 23 stat +/- 23 sys keV and 2.84 tonne-year.

2. Why the neutrino lines are 475 and 557 keV (f-025; Fig. 2 of 2609.01590, Figs. 2-3 of 2609.07807). The difference comes from how the captured higgsinos are treated in the Sun, not from the halo model.
- 2609.01590, at m_chi = 1.11 TeV: if elastic scattering is negligible (the blind spot), the captured higgsinos never thermalize and stay on extended orbits, so they annihilate less. With <sigma v>_eff of about 1.5e-26 cm^3/s and ten years of IceCube data, this excludes delta_m up to about 475 keV at 90% CL. Loose solar and nuclear inputs lower this to 466 keV, and the Fe nuclear-response uncertainty to about 454 keV. If elastic scattering lets them reach equilibrium, the same paper finds delta_m >~ 553 keV.
- 2609.07807 assumes the captured higgsinos thermalize and uses a standard truncated Maxwellian halo: u0 = 220 km/s, v_esc = 544 km/s, v_sun = 232 km/s, rho = 0.4 GeV/cm^3. Other inputs are sigma_chi_n = 7.4e-39 cm^2, <sigma v> = 1.3e-26 cm^3/s and m_chi = 1.08 TeV, with a 95% CL fit to IceCube nu_mu, IceCube nu_e and Super-K data. It excludes delta_m below about 557 keV, which agrees with the 553 keV equilibrium result. It still allows rescue by an LMC tail or substructure.

3. Gamma-ray lines near 1.1 TeV, 2609.01590 (f-026, Fig. 3). The thermal prediction is 0.815-0.900 of the H.E.S.S. 546 h limits, which the paper calls close to, but not excluded by, the present limits. The CTAO Alpha 500 h projection, mu_gamma,95 = 1.69, falls short of the thermal target. The Omega configuration, estimated at 0.85, would reach it. Dwarf-galaxy, CMB and ATLAS disappearing-track limits do not exclude the region.

4. Rescue and alternative scenarios, abstracts only (f-027).
- 2610.03692: the 1.1 TeV thermal higgsino is only marginally compatible with the LZ event and IceCube, and only with the LMC tail, no elastic cooling in the Sun and no sideband constraint. Compatible regions run from about 2 TeV to hundreds of TeV, with delta about 350-525 keV.
- 2609.09830: one-loop electroweak corrections with on-shell renormalization reduce delta_m. The abstract gives no size for the change.
- 2609.06890: light boosted dark matter, which does not depend on the halo velocity tail.

Still open (q-16): how large the 2609.09830 radiative correction is, and the numbers for the four IceCube variants in 2610.03692.

Title: The last Complex WIMPs standing
Authors: Salvatore Bottaro, Dario Buttazzo, Marco Costa, Roberto Franceschini, Paolo Panci, Diego Redigolo, Ludovico Vittorio
Year: 2022
arXiv ID: 2205.04486

============================================================

--- Page 1 ---
CERN-TH-2022-080
The last Complex WIMPs standing
Salvatore Bottaro, 1, 2 Dario Buttazzo, 2 Marco Costa, 1, 2 Roberto
Franceschini,3 Paolo Panci,4, 2 Diego Redigolo, 5, 6 and Ludovico Vittorio 1, 2
1Scuola Normale Superiore, Piazza dei Cavalieri 7, 56126 Pisa, Italy
2INFN, Sezione di Pisa, Largo Bruno Pontecorvo 3, I-56127 Pisa, Italy
3Universit` a degli Studi and INFN Roma Tre, Via della Vasca Navale 84, I-00146, Rome
4Dipartimento di Fisica E. Fermi, Universit` a di Pisa, Largo B. Pontecorvo 3, I-56127 Pisa, Italy
5CERN, Theoretical Physics Department, Geneva, Switzerland.
6INFN, Sezione di Firenze Via G. Sansone 1, 50019 Sesto Fiorentino, Italy
(Dated: May 11, 2022)
We continue the study of weakly interacting massive particles (WIMP) started in [1], focusing
on a single complex electroweak n-plet with non-zero hypercharge added to the Standard Model.
The minimal splitting between the Dark Matter and its electroweak neutral partner required to
circumvent direct detection constraints allows only multiplets with hypercharge smaller or equal to
1. We compute for the ﬁrst time all the calculable WIMP masses up to the largest multiplet allowed
by perturbative unitarity. For the minimal allowed splitting, most of these multiplets can be fully
probed at future large-exposure direct detection experiments, with the notable exception of the
doublet with hypercharge 1/2. We show how a future muon collider can fully explore the parameter
space of the complex doublet combining missing mass, displaced track and long-lived track searches.
In the same spirit, we study how a future muon collider can probe the parameter space of complex
WIMPs in regions where the direct detection cross section drops below the neutrino ﬂoor. Finally,
we comment on how precision observables can provide additional constraints on complex WIMPs.
I. INTRODUCTION
Despite the intense experimental activity in the past
50 years, the possibility that Dark Matter (DM) is a
new weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) re-
mains open today. Within this framework, the most
minimal and predictive possibility is that the DM is
the lightest neutral component of a single electroweak
(EW) multiplet. In this simpliﬁed setup, the exper-
imentally viable DM candidates can be fully clas-
siﬁed and their thermal masses predicted once the
relic abundance from freeze-out is required to match
the observed DM density today Ω DMh2 = 0.11933±
0.00091 [2].
Experimentally, direct detection (DD) experiments
robustly excluded the possibility that DM has tree-
level Z-mediated interactions with the nuclei. This
experimental milestone left only two possible scenar-
ios for EW WIMPs wide open: i) WIMPs with zero
hypercharge (Y = 0), interacting with nucleons only

processes may provide a promising avenue, along with the elastic scattering, when the mass
splitting between the neutral Higgsino pairs is extremely tiny. The mass splitting can be re-

in the MSSM. Moreover, all the one-loop electroweak (EW) corrections to the three-point
vertices for the neutralino(s)-Higgs interactions have been considered, while both elastic

recoil event of interest reported by the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, taking into account IceCube

searches, both with and without including a constraint from the absence of events in the LZ high-
energy sideband. In our LZ analysis, we consider the DM distribution in the Standard Halo Model
alone as well as possible enhancements of the high-speed tail induced by the Large Magellanic Cloud
(LMC). We present four variants of bounds from IceCube on Higgsino dark matter, depending on
various assumptions on cooling channels in the Sun, motivated by severe theoretical uncertainties
about Higgsino-nucleon elastic scattering (unimportant for direct detection but crucial for IceCube
bounds). Whereas the thermal Higgsino with a mass of 1.1 TeV remains only marginally compatible
with both the LZ event and the IceCube limits when the LMC-induced high-speed tail is included
and both elastic cooling in the Sun and the LZ high-energy sideband constraint are neglected, higher

Standard Model (BSM) of particle physics.
Direct detection laboratory experiments, originally
proposed in the 1980s [1, 2], are designed to probe the

terrestrial detectors situated deep underground. Despite
decades of experimental searches with continuously im-

NaI detectors consistent with a WIMP interpretation[3],
but these results are in tension with recent experiments
made of the same material [4].

Direct detection rate of heavy Higgsino-like and Wino-like
dark matter
Qing Chen 1 and Richard J. Hill 1,2
1Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Kentucky, Lexington, KY 40506, USA
2Theoretical Physics Department, Fermilab, Batavia, IL 60510, USA
March 19, 2020
Abstract
Many viable dark matter models contain a WIMP candidate that is a component of a new elec-
troweak multiplet whose massM is large compared to the electroweak scalemW . A generic amplitude-
level cancellation in such models yields a severe suppression of the cross section for WIMP-nucleon
scattering, making it important to assess the impact of formally subleading eﬀects. The power cor-
rection of order mW/M to the heavy WIMP limit is computed for electroweak doublet (Higgsino-like)
dark matter candidates, and a modern model of nuclear modiﬁcations to the free nucleon cross section
is evaluated. Corrections to the pure Higgsino limit are determined by a single parameter through ﬁrst
order in the heavy WIMP expansion. Current and projected experimental bounds on this parameter
are investigated. The direct detection signal in the pure Higgsino limit remains below neutrino back-
grounds for WIMPs in the TeV mass range. Nuclear corrections are applied also to the heavy Wino
case, completing the investigation of combined subleading eﬀects from perturbative QCD, 1 /M power
corrections, and nuclear modiﬁcations.

The LZ analysis adopted the standard astrophysical

high energy recoil events can be very sensitive to the
high-speed tail of the local DM distribution, which is
not well-known. The interaction of our dark matter halo
with neighbor halos, such as the Large Magellanic Cloud
(LMC) [33, 35], can accelerate the DM particles in our
halo and allow high-speed DM particles from neighboring
halos to enter ours as well as gravitationally significantly
enhance the high-speed tail of the local DM distribution.
Including the effects of the LMC is particularly impor-

earlier paper [6], we took into account only the WIMPs

provides no information beyondv min ≃950 km/s, we
conservatively setη(v min) = 0 above this value.

tion of results and their implications.
•We identify the region of parameter space corresponding to a Higgsino-like neutralino LSP,

becomes comparable in significance to the elastic scattering channel. For such small mass

V. HIGH-ENERGY SIDEBAND IN LZ DA T A
Rodd et al. suggested that any explanation of the LZ
event atδ= 350 keV should also be consistent with the
lack of events in the LZ experiment at higher energies,
in its “sideband” at recoil energies∼350–650 keV [14].
However, the LZ collaboration has not published the ac-
ceptance in this sideband and did not include it in the
DM signal likelihood. The nuclear recoil response of the
detector up at those high recoil energies has not yet been
calibrated and is the subject of current work by the LZ
collaboration. Hence in this paper we will present results
both with and without the empty sideband taken into
account.
In those cases where we do require compatibilty of
our model with an empty sideband, we extend our LZ
likelihood to include the sideband. We can then iden-
tify regions in the (m χ,δ) plane compatible with the
LZ region of interest (ROI) as well as the empty side-
band. We extend our 96-bin likelihood by a Poisson
factorL SB = exp(−N SB), modeling the sideband as
350< E R <650 keV with zero observed events, zero
expected background, and unit signal acceptance. Here
NSB is the predicted differential recoil rate integrated
over this interval and multiplied by the exposure. Be-
cause the acceptance for DM-induced recoils in the exper-
imental sideband has not been published, the resulting
constraint is conditional on our acceptance and energy-
window approximations [14].
Fig. 2 illustrates the effect of the sideband on the LZ
confidence regions at 90% CL in the Higgsino parameter
space. The upper (lower) panel uses the SHM (SHM +
LMC) velocity distribution for the LZ prediction. Or-
ange dashed and blue solid contours show the approx-
imate joint 90% confidence regions in (m χ,δ) obtained
from our likelihood analysis with and without the high-
energy sideband, respectively, at fixed Higgsino coupling.
The star and diamond mark the corresponding best-fit
points, respectively. We note that there are two regions
compatible with empty sideband events. One region cor-
responds to lower DM massm χ <1 TeV, in which case
very few high energy recoil events are produced; but this
low mass region is ruled out by IceCube neutrino bounds
described in the next Section. The second region cor-
responds to higher Higgsino mass, and it is compatible
with the empty sideband because the particle abundance
and hence expected count rate decreases∼1/m χ.
In the rest of the paper we will present results both
with and without the empty sideband taken into account.

VI. SOLAR BOUNDS FROM NEUTRINO
TELESCOPES
Neutrino telescopes provide complementary probes of
dark matter particles through searches for neutrinos from
DM annihilation in the Sun 7. In particular, the absence
of a neutrino excess from the direction of the Sun in Ice-
Cube and Super-Kamiokande places strong constraints
on the DM particles studied in this paper. The same
inelastic DM–nucleus scattering process that could ex-
plain the LZ event can also occur as DM traverses the
Sun. Inelastic interactions with solar nuclei cause DM
particles to lose energy, allowing some to become gravi-
tationally bound to the Sun when their speeds fall below
the local solar escape speed. Because the solar gravi-
tational field accelerates incident DM particles, inelastic
scattering on heavy solar nuclei can occur at mass split-
tings beyond the reach of terrestrial xenon experiments.
Once captured, DM particles can cool by losing energy
through repeated scattering with solar nuclei. Inelas-
tic cooling stops when scattering becomes kinematically
inaccessible, while elastic interactions can allow further
energy loss. This cooling concentrates the captured pop-
ulation closer to the solar center, increasing its density
and enhancing the annihilation rate. If the Higgsino in-
teractions are sufficiently effective, cooling can proceed
rapidly enough for Higgsino capture and annihilation to
approach equilibrium. Capture–annihilation equilibrium
implies that the number of Higgsinos captured per unit
time equals the number lost to annihilation, yielding the
maximum annihilation rate sustained by a capture rate.
Understanding when cooling becomes inefficient or ceases
is essential, as well as identifying whether or not capture–
annihilation equilibrium is reached. DM annihilation in
the Sun produces neutrinos that can be detected by neu-
trino telescopes. The absence of a DM-induced solar neu-
trino excess in IceCube can therefore constrain Higgsino
properties, specifically the particle mass and mass split-
ting [12, 13]. Here we estimate these constraints under
different assumptions about the interactions responsible

args.claim: Inverting the kinematics at m_chi = 1100 GeV gives the v_max (Earth frame) needed to reach a given delta with an event exactly at E_R = 248 keV: 893 km/s for 457 keV, 915 km/s for 475 keV, 968 km/s for 519 keV, 980 km/s for 529 keV and 1015 km/s for 557 keV (about +3 km/s at 1000 GeV, about -2 km/s at 1183 GeV). If E_R is free (at the optimal E_R = mu*delta/m_N of about 380-500 keV), the minimum is v_max = sqrt(2 delta/mu): 830 km/s for 422, 864 for 457, 881 for 475, 921 for 519, 930 for 529 and 954 km/s for 557 keV. All of these exceed the tool's SHM cutoff of 776 km/s by 55-240 km/s. So the 2609.01590 profiled-Maxwellian upper edges (422/457 keV) imply an effective endpoint of about 830-890 km/s. The Halo 13 edges (519/529 keV) need about 920-980 km/s of LMC-boosted tail. Covering delta >= 557 keV (above the Super-K + IceCube line) needs at least about 950-1015 km/s, and delta >= 475 keV needs at least about 880-915 km/s. The higgsino reading therefore rests entirely on the halo's population above about 880 km/s in the Earth frame.
args.note: Hand-computed inversion, consistent with tool v_min(248 keV) = 921/969/1018 km/s at 480/520/560 keV (f-018). Comparing with the v_esc + v_E actually used in 2609.01590's halos was not possible within budget; the paper's endpoint values have no validated quote (x-04). The E_R uncertainty (+/-33 keV combined) moves the 248 keV numbers toward the E_R-optimized ones.

delta:
**Completed — Run an analytic and tool-based kinematic check of delta_max(m_chi, v_max) at E_R = 248 keV. Identify the scan points compatible with the LZ event, and reconcile the tool's 776 km/s cutoff with the upper delta edges of 2609.01590 (profiled Maxwellian 422/457 keV; Halo 13 519/529 keV)..** Main result: under the tool's halo, which cuts off at 776 km/s, no point that reproduces the LZ event has delta of 475 keV or more; the compatible band sits at about 350 keV. Everything ran locally. Points in the 0.3-5 event band were identified by bracketing with predict_recoil, because the scan file could not be read (x-07).

Event counts from predict_recoil (LZ, 2.84 t-yr):
- delta 340 keV: 10.67 events at 1000 GeV and 17.30 at 1183 GeV
- delta 350 keV: 1.13 at 1000 GeV and 2.90 at 1200 GeV
- delta 360 keV: 0.03 at 1000 GeV and 0.158 at 1183 GeV
- delta 380 keV: 0.00 at both masses

A new 16x16 scan (m_chi 1000-1200 GeV, delta 330-480 keV in 10 keV steps) passes all 256 points and puts 16 in the 0.3-5 band, best fit (1000 GeV, 350 keV). That the 16 are the delta = 350 keV row is inferred from the bracketing, not listed by the tool (f-032). This scan overwrote /Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/scan_idm.npz and constraint_summary.png. The tools return no figure numbers.

Analytic check (f-033, hand-computed): delta_max = v_max*sqrt(2 m_N E_R) - m_N E_R/mu at E_R = 248 keV, with m_N = 122 GeV. At 1000/1100/1183 GeV it gives 358.5/361.3/363.2 keV for 776 km/s, 378/381/383 keV for 800, 419/422/424 keV for 850 and 460/463/465 keV for 900 km/s. It matches the tool's v_min(248 keV) to within about 1 km/s. The tool's 'about 365 keV' edge is the endpoint when E_R is left free, mu v^2/2 = 364-370 keV at 776 km/s, reached near E_R of about 330 keV rather than at 248 keV.

Required v_max (f-034, hand-computed), at 1100 GeV with the event at 248 keV: 893 km/s for 457 keV, 915 for 475, 968 for 519, 980 for 529 and 1015 for 557 keV. With E_R left free the minimum is lower: 830 km/s for 422 keV, 864 for 457, 881 for 475, 921 for 519, 930 for 529 and 954 for 557 keV.

What this means for 2609.01590 and the LMC tail:
- The paper's profiled-Maxwellian upper edges (422/457 keV) imply an effective endpoint of about 830-890 km/s, compared with the tool's 776 km/s. This explains why the tool gives zero events at 400 keV.
- The Halo 13 edges (519/529 keV) need an LMC-boosted tail reaching about 920-980 km/s.
- Clearing the 475 keV IceCube line needs at least about 880-915 km/s.
- Clearing the 557 keV Super-K + IceCube line needs at least about 950-1015 km/s.
The higgsino reading of the event therefore depends entirely on how many particles the halo has above about 880 km/s in the Earth frame.
